Installation Essentials Start coding! 🚀 In-depth Guides Signals Updated Components Templates Directives Dependency Injection Updated Routing Forms Updated HTTP Client Server-side &amp; hybrid-rendering Testing Angular Aria New Internationalization Animations Drag and drop Build with AI Get Started LLM prompts and AI IDE setup Agent Skills New Angular CLI MCP Server setup Angular AI Tutor Design Patterns WebMCP New Developer Tools Angular CLI Libraries DevTools Language Service Best Practices Style Guide Security Accessibility Unhandled errors in Angular Performance Keeping up-to-date Developer Events Angular v22 Release New Angular v21 Release Extended Ecosystem NgModules Legacy Animations Using RxJS with Angular Service Workers &amp; PWAs Web workers Custom build pipeline Tailwind Angular Fire Google Maps Google Pay YouTube player Angular CDK Angular Material arrow_back Angular CLI Overview Local set-up Building Angular apps Serving Angular apps for development Deployment End-to-End Testing Migrating to new build system Build environments Angular CLI builders Generating code using schematics Authoring schematics Schematics for libraries Template type checking Ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation AOT metadata errors Developer Tools Angular CLI Template type checking On this page arrow_upward_alt Back to the top Overview of template type checking Just as TypeScript catches type errors in your code, Angular checks the expressions and bindings within the templates of your application and can report any type errors it finds. Angular has two modes of doing this, depending on the value of the strictTemplates flag in Angular's compiler options . Basic mode In the basic type-checking mode, with the strictTemplates flag set to false , Angular validates only top-level expressions in a template. If you write &lt;map [city]="user.address.city"&gt; , the compiler verifies the following: user is a property on the component class user is an object with an address property user.address is an object with a city property The compiler does not verify that the value of user.address.city is assignable to the city input of the &lt;map&gt; component. The compiler also has some major limitations in this mode: Importantly, it doesn't check embedded views, such as *ngIf , *ngFor , other &lt;ng-template&gt; embedded view. It doesn't figure out the types of #refs , the results of pipes, or the type of $event in event bindings. In many cases, these things end up as type any , which can cause subsequent parts of the expression to go unchecked. Strict mode Strict mode is the default, and is enabled when the strictTemplates flag is true or not set. In strict mode, Angular does the following: Checks embedded views (such as those within an *ngIf or *ngFor ) Infers the correct return type of pipes Infers the correct type of local references to directives and pipes Verifies that component/directive bindings are assignable to their input() s Obeys TypeScript's strictNullChecks flag when validating input bindings Infers the correct type of components/directives, including generics Infers template context types where configured (for example, allowing correct type-checking of NgFor ) Infers the correct type of $event in component/directive, DOM, and animation event bindings Infers the correct type of local references to DOM elements, based on the tag name (for example, the type that document.createElement would return for that tag) Checking of *ngFor The two modes of type-checking treat embedded views differently. Consider the following example. User interface interface User { name : string ; address : { city : string ; state : string ; }; } &lt; div * ngFor = "let user of users" &gt; &lt; h2 &gt;{{config.title}}&lt;/ h2 &gt; &lt; span &gt;City: {{user.address.city}}&lt;/ span &gt; &lt;/ div &gt; The &lt;h2&gt; and the &lt;span&gt; are in the *ngFor embedded view. In basic mode, Angular doesn't check either of them. In strict mode, Angular knows that the user in the &lt;span&gt; has a type of User , and that address is an object with a city property of type string . Troubleshooting template errors With strict mode, you might encounter template errors that didn't arise in basic mode. These errors often represent genuine type mismatches in the templates that were not caught by the previous tooling. If this is the case, the error message should make it clear where in the template the problem occurs. There can also be false positives when the typings of an Angular library are either incomplete or incorrect, or when the typings don't quite line up with expectations as in the following cases. When a library's typings are wrong or incomplete (for example, missing null | undefined if the library was not written with strictNullChecks in mind) When a library's input types are too narrow and the library hasn't added appropriate metadata for Angular to figure this out. This usually occurs with disabled or other common Boolean inputs used as attributes, for example, &lt;input disabled&gt; . When using $event.target for DOM events (because of the possibility of event bubbling, $event.target in the DOM typings doesn't have the type you might expect) In case of a false positive like these, there are a few options: Use the $any() type-cast function in certain contexts to opt out of type-checking for a part of the expression Disable strict checks entirely by setting strictTemplates: false in the application's TypeScript configuration file, tsconfig.json Disable certain type-checking operations individually, while maintaining strictness in other aspects, by setting a strictness flag to false If you want to use strictTemplates and strictNullChecks together, opt out of strict null type checking specifically for input bindings using strictNullInputTypes Each following option is set to the value for strictTemplates ( true when strictTemplates is true and conversely, the other way around): Strictness flag Effect strictInputTypes Whether the assignability of a binding expression to the @Input() field is checked. Also affects the inference of directive generic types. strictNullInputTypes Whether strictNullChecks is honored when checking @Input() bindings (per strictInputTypes ). Turning this off can be useful when using a library that was not built with strictNullChecks in mind. strictAttributeTypes Whether to check @Input() bindings that are made using text attributes. For example, &lt;input matInput disabled="true"&gt; (setting the disabled property to the string 'true' ) vs &lt;input matInput [disabled]="true"&gt; (setting the disabled property to the boolean true ). strictSafeNavigationTypes Whether the return type of safe navigation operations (for example, user?.name will be correctly inferred based on the type of user ). If disabled, user?.name will be of type any . strictDomLocalRefTypes Whether local references to DOM elements will have the correct type. If disabled ref will be of type any for &lt;input #ref&gt; . strictOutputEventTypes Whether $event will have the correct type for event bindings to component/directive an @Output() , or to animation events. If disabled, it will be any . strictDomEventTypes Whether $event will have the correct type for event bindings to DOM events. If disabled, it will be any . strictContextGenerics Whether the type parameters of generic components will be inferred correctly (including any generic bounds). If disabled, any type parameters will be any . strictLiteralTypes Whether object and array literals declared in the template will have their type inferred. If disabled, the type of such literals will be any . Strictness flag Effect :--------------------------- :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- strictInputAccessModifiers Whether access modifiers such as private / protected / readonly are honored when assigning a binding expression to an @Input() or input() . If disabled, the access modifiers of the input are ignored; only the type is checked. Note: This checking only applies to inputs, not outputs. strictUnclaimedEventNames Whether to report event bindings whose name matches neither an output of a directive applied to the element nor a known native DOM event — the ones described by TypeScript's GlobalEventHandlersEventMap , compared ignoring case — which usually indicates a misspelled output name. Only single-identifier camelCase names are checked; dash-separated names (for example, my-event ), which custom events dispatched by descendants conventionally use, are exempt, as are elements without a matched component when CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA is in use. This option is false by default, even with strictTemplates set to true . If you still have issues after troubleshooting with these flags, an option of last resort is to fall back to basic mode by disabling strictTemplates . A type-checking error that you cannot resolve with any of the recommended methods can be the result of a bug in the template type-checker itself. If you get errors that require falling back to basic mode, it is likely to be such a bug. If this happens, file an issue so the team can address it. Inputs and type-checking The template type checker checks whether a binding expression's type is compatible with that of the corresponding directive input. As an example, consider the following component: export interface User { name : string ; } @ Component ({ selector: 'user-detail' , template: ' {{ user ().name }} ' , }) export class UserDetailComponent { user = input. required &lt; User &gt;(); } The AppComponent template uses this component as follows: @ Component ({ selector: 'app-root' , template: ' &lt; user-detail [user] = "selectedUser" &gt;&lt;/ user-detail &gt; ' , }) export class AppComponent { selectedUser : User | null = null ; } Here, during type checking of the template for AppComponent , the [user]="selectedUser" binding corresponds with the UserDetailComponent.user input. Therefore, Angular assigns the selectedUser property to UserDetailComponent.user , which would result in an error if their types were incompatible. TypeScript checks the assignment according to its type system, obeying flags such as strictNullChecks as they are configured in the application. Avoid run-time type errors by providing more specific in-template type requirements to the template type checker. Make the input type requirements for your own directives as specific as possible by providing template-guard functions in the directive definition. See Improving template type checking for custom directives in this guide. Strict null checks When you enable strictTemplates and the TypeScript flag strictNullChecks , typecheck errors might occur for certain situations that might not easily be avoided. For example: A nullable value that is bound to a directive from a library which did not have strictNullChecks enabled. For a library compiled without strictNullChecks , its declaration files will not indicate whether a field can be null or not. For situations where the library handles null correctly, this is problematic, as the compiler will check a nullable value against the declaration files which omit the null type. As such, the compiler produces a type-check error because it adheres to strictNullChecks . Using the async pipe with an Observable which you know will emit synchronously. The async pipe currently assumes that the Observable it subscribes to can be asynchronous, which means that it's possible that there is no value available yet. In that case, it still has to return something —which is null . In other words, the return type of the async pipe includes null , which might result in errors in situations where the Observable is known to emit a non-nullable value synchronously. There are two potential workarounds to the preceding issues: In the template, include the non-null assertion operator ! at the end of a nullable expression, such as &lt; user-detail [user] = "user!" &gt;&lt;/ user-detail &gt; In this example, the compiler disregards type incompatibilities in nullability, just as in TypeScript code. In the case of the async pipe, notice that the expression needs to be wrapped in parentheses, as in &lt; user-detail [user] = "(user$ | async)!" &gt;&lt;/ user-detail &gt; Disable strict null checks in Angular templates completely. When strictTemplates is enabled, it is still possible to disable certain aspects of type checking. Setting the option strictNullInputTypes to false disables strict null checks within Angular templates. This flag applies for all components that are part of the application. Advice for library authors As a library author, you can take several measures to provide an optimal experience for your users. First, enabling strictNullChecks and including null in an input's type, as appropriate, communicates to your consumers whether they can provide a nullable value or not. Additionally, it is possible to provide type hints that are specific to the template type checker. See Improving template type checking for custom directives , and Input setter coercion . Input setter coercion Occasionally it is desirable for the input() property of a directive or component to alter the value bound to it, typically using a transform function for the input. As an example, consider this custom button component: Consider the following directive: @ Component ({ selector: ' submit -button' , template: ` &lt; div class = "wrapper" &gt; &lt; button [disabled] = "disabled()" &gt;Submit&lt;/ button &gt; &lt;/ div &gt; ` , }) class SubmitButton { disabled = input. required ({transform: booleanAttribute }); } Here, the disabled input of the component is being passed on to the &lt;button&gt; in the template. All of this works as expected, as long as a boolean value is bound to the input. But, suppose a consumer uses this input in the template as an attribute: &lt; submit -button disabled &gt;&lt;/ submit -button &gt; This has the same effect as the binding: &lt; submit -button [disabled] = "''" &gt;&lt;/ submit -button &gt; At runtime, the input will be set to the empty string, which is not a boolean value. Angular component libraries that deal with this problem often "coerce" the value into the right type in the setter: set disabled (value: boolean) { this ._disabled = (value === '' ) || value; } It would be ideal to change the type of value here, from boolean to boolean|'' , to match the set of values which are actually accepted by the setter. TypeScript prior to version 4.3 requires that both the getter and setter have the same type, so if the getter should return a boolean then the setter is stuck with the narrower type. If the consumer has Angular's strictest type checking for templates enabled, this creates a problem: the empty string ( '' ) is not actually assignable to the disabled field, which creates a type error when the attribute form is used. As a workaround for this problem, Angular supports checking a wider, more permissive type for @Input() than is declared for the input field itself. Enable this by adding a static property with the ngAcceptInputType_ prefix to the component class: class SubmitButton { private _disabled : boolean ; @ Input () get disabled () : boolean { return this ._disabled; } set disabled ( value : boolean ) { this ._disabled = value === '' || value; } static ngAcceptInputType_disabled : boolean | '' ; } Since TypeScript 4.3, the setter could have been declared to accept boolean|'' as type, making the input setter coercion field obsolete. As such, input setters coercion fields have been deprecated. This field does not need to have a value. Its existence communicates to the Angular type checker that the disabled input should be considered as accepting bindings that match the type boolean|'' . The suffix should be the @Input field name. Care should be taken that if an ngAcceptInputType_ override is present for a given input, then the setter should be able to handle any values of the overridden type. Disabling type checking using $any() Disable checking of a binding expression by surrounding the expression in a call to the $any() cast pseudo-function. The compiler treats it as a cast to the any type just like in TypeScript when a &lt;any&gt; or as any cast is used. In the following example, casting person to the any type suppresses the error Property address does not exist . @ Component ({ selector: 'my-component' , template: ' {{ $any (person).address.street}} ' , }) class MyComponent { person ?: Person ; } Social Media Blog X (formerly Twitter) Bluesky YouTube Discord GitHub Stack Overflow Community Contribute Code of Conduct Report Issues Google's DevLibrary Angular Google Developer Experts Resources Press Kit Roadmap Community translations Azərbaycanca Español Türkçe Русский 한국어 日本語版 简体中文版 正體中文版 Super-powered by Google ©2010-2026. style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\n\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\"> &lt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">h2\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;{{config.title}}&lt;\u002F\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">h2\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\n\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\"> &lt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">span\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;City: {{user.address.city}}&lt;\u002F\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">span\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\n\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&lt;\u002F\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">div\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fpre>\n \u003C\u002Fdiv>\u003Cp>The \u003Ccode>&lt;h2&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode> and the \u003Ccode>&lt;span&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode> are in the \u003Ccode>*ngFor\u003C\u002Fcode> embedded view.\nIn basic mode, Angular doesn't check either of them.\nIn strict mode, Angular knows that the \u003Ccode>user\u003C\u002Fcode> in the \u003Ccode>&lt;span&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode> has a type of \u003Ccode>User\u003C\u002Fcode>, and that \u003Ccode>address\u003C\u002Fcode> is an object with a \u003Ccode>city\u003C\u002Fcode> property of type \u003Ccode>string\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Ch2 id=\"troubleshooting-template-errors\">\n \u003Ca href=\"#troubleshooting-template-errors\" class=\"docs-anchor\" tabindex=\"-1\" aria-label=\"Link to Troubleshooting template errors\">Troubleshooting template errors\u003C\u002Fa>\n \u003C\u002Fh2>\n \u003Cp>With strict mode, you might encounter template errors that didn't arise in basic mode.\nThese errors often represent genuine type mismatches in the templates that were not caught by the previous tooling.\nIf this is the case, the error message should make it clear where in the template the problem occurs.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>There can also be false positives when the typings of an Angular library are either incomplete or incorrect, or when the typings don't quite line up with expectations as in the following cases.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Cul class=\"docs-list\">\n \u003Cli>\u003Cp>When a library's typings are wrong or incomplete (for example, missing \u003Ccode>null | undefined\u003C\u002Fcode> if the library was not written with \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode> in mind)\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003C\u002Fli>\n\u003Cli>\u003Cp>When a library's input types are too narrow and the library hasn't added appropriate metadata for Angular to figure this out.\nThis usually occurs with disabled or other common Boolean inputs used as attributes, for example, \u003Ccode>&lt;input disabled&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003C\u002Fli>\n\u003Cli>\u003Cp>When using \u003Ccode>$event.target\u003C\u002Fcode> for DOM events (because of the possibility of event bubbling, \u003Ccode>$event.target\u003C\u002Fcode> in the DOM typings doesn't have the type you might expect)\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003C\u002Fli>\n\n \u003C\u002Ful>\n \u003Cp>In case of a false positive like these, there are a few options:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Cul class=\"docs-list\">\n \u003Cli>Use the \u003Ccode>$any()\u003C\u002Fcode> type-cast function in certain contexts to opt out of type-checking for a part of the expression\u003C\u002Fli>\n\u003Cli>Disable strict checks entirely by setting \u003Ccode>strictTemplates: false\u003C\u002Fcode> in the application's TypeScript configuration file, \u003Ccode>tsconfig.json\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fli>\n\u003Cli>Disable certain type-checking operations individually, while maintaining strictness in other aspects, by setting a \u003Cem>strictness flag\u003C\u002Fem> to \u003Ccode>false\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fli>\n\u003Cli>If you want to use \u003Ccode>strictTemplates\u003C\u002Fcode> and \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode> together, opt out of strict null type checking specifically for input bindings using \u003Ccode>strictNullInputTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fli>\n\n \u003C\u002Ful>\n \u003Cp>Each following option is set to the value for \u003Ccode>strictTemplates\u003C\u002Fcode> (\u003Ccode>true\u003C\u002Fcode> when \u003Ccode>strictTemplates\u003C\u002Fcode> is \u003Ccode>true\u003C\u002Fcode> and conversely, the other way around):\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Cdiv class=\"docs-table docs-scroll-track-transparent\">\n \u003Ctable>\n \u003Cthead>\n \u003Ctr>\n\u003Cth align=\"left\">Strictness flag\u003C\u002Fth>\n\u003Cth align=\"left\">Effect\u003C\u002Fth>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\n \u003C\u002Fthead>\n \u003Ctbody>\n \u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictInputTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether the assignability of a binding expression to the \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002FInput\">\u003Ccode>@Input()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa> field is checked. Also affects the inference of directive generic types.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictNullInputTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode> is honored when checking \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002FInput\">\u003Ccode>@Input()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa> bindings (per \u003Ccode>strictInputTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>). Turning this off can be useful when using a library that was not built with \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode> in mind.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictAttributeTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether to check \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002FInput\">\u003Ccode>@Input()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa> bindings that are made using text attributes. For example, \u003Ccode>&lt;input matInput disabled=&quot;true&quot;&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode> (setting the \u003Ccode>disabled\u003C\u002Fcode> property to the string \u003Ccode>&#39;true&#39;\u003C\u002Fcode>) vs \u003Ccode>&lt;input matInput [disabled]=&quot;true&quot;&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode> (setting the \u003Ccode>disabled\u003C\u002Fcode> property to the boolean \u003Ccode>true\u003C\u002Fcode>).\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictSafeNavigationTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether the return type of safe navigation operations (for example, \u003Ccode>user?.name\u003C\u002Fcode> will be correctly inferred based on the type of \u003Ccode>user\u003C\u002Fcode>). If disabled, \u003Ccode>user?.name\u003C\u002Fcode> will be of type \u003Ccode>any\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictDomLocalRefTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether local references to DOM elements will have the correct type. If disabled \u003Ccode>ref\u003C\u002Fcode> will be of type \u003Ccode>any\u003C\u002Fcode> for \u003Ccode>&lt;input #ref&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictOutputEventTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether \u003Ccode>$event\u003C\u002Fcode> will have the correct type for event bindings to component\u002Fdirective an \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002FOutput\">\u003Ccode>@Output()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa>, or to animation events. If disabled, it will be \u003Ccode>any\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictDomEventTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether \u003Ccode>$event\u003C\u002Fcode> will have the correct type for event bindings to DOM events. If disabled, it will be \u003Ccode>any\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictContextGenerics\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether the type parameters of generic components will be inferred correctly (including any generic bounds). If disabled, any type parameters will be \u003Ccode>any\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictLiteralTypes\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether object and array literals declared in the template will have their type inferred. If disabled, the type of such literals will be \u003Ccode>any\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Strictness flag\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Effect\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">:---------------------------\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictInputAccessModifiers\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether access modifiers such as \u003Ccode>private\u003C\u002Fcode>\u002F\u003Ccode>protected\u003C\u002Fcode>\u002F\u003Ccode>readonly\u003C\u002Fcode> are honored when assigning a binding expression to an \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002FInput\">\u003Ccode>@Input()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa> or \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002Finput\">\u003Ccode>input()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa>. If disabled, the access modifiers of the input are ignored; only the type is checked. Note: This checking only applies to inputs, not outputs.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\u003Ctr>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">\u003Ccode>strictUnclaimedEventNames\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003Ctd align=\"left\">Whether to report event bindings whose name matches neither an output of a directive applied to the element nor a known native DOM event — the ones described by TypeScript's \u003Ccode>GlobalEventHandlersEventMap\u003C\u002Fcode>, compared ignoring case — which usually indicates a misspelled output name. Only single-identifier camelCase names are checked; dash-separated names (for example, \u003Ccode>my-event\u003C\u002Fcode>), which custom events dispatched by descendants conventionally use, are exempt, as are elements without a matched component when \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002FCUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA\">\u003Ccode>CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa> is in use. This option is \u003Ccode>false\u003C\u002Fcode> by default, even with \u003Ccode>strictTemplates\u003C\u002Fcode> set to \u003Ccode>true\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Ftd>\n\u003C\u002Ftr>\n\n \u003C\u002Ftbody>\n \u003C\u002Ftable>\n \u003C\u002Fdiv>\n \u003Cp>If you still have issues after troubleshooting with these flags, an option of last resort is to fall back to basic mode by disabling \u003Ccode>strictTemplates\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>A type-checking error that you cannot resolve with any of the recommended methods can be the result of a bug in the template type-checker itself.\nIf you get errors that require falling back to basic mode, it is likely to be such a bug.\nIf this happens, \u003Ca href=\"https:\u002F\u002Fgithub.com\u002Fangular\u002Fangular\u002Fissues\" target=\"_blank\">file an issue\u003C\u002Fa> so the team can address it.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Ch2 id=\"inputs-and-type-checking\">\n \u003Ca href=\"#inputs-and-type-checking\" class=\"docs-anchor\" tabindex=\"-1\" aria-label=\"Link to Inputs and type-checking\">Inputs and type-checking\u003C\u002Fa>\n \u003C\u002Fh2>\n \u003Cp>The template type checker checks whether a binding expression's type is compatible with that of the corresponding directive input.\nAs an style=\"--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583\"> |\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF\"> null\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583\"> =\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF\"> null\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\n\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">}\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fpre>\n \u003C\u002Fdiv>\u003Cp>Here, during type checking of the template for \u003Ccode>AppComponent\u003C\u002Fcode>, the \u003Ccode>[user]=&quot;selectedUser&quot;\u003C\u002Fcode> binding corresponds with the \u003Ccode>UserDetailComponent.user\u003C\u002Fcode> input.\nTherefore, Angular assigns the \u003Ccode>selectedUser\u003C\u002Fcode> property to \u003Ccode>UserDetailComponent.user\u003C\u002Fcode>, which would result in an error if their types were incompatible.\nTypeScript checks the assignment according to its type system, obeying flags such as \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode> as they are configured in the application.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>Avoid run-time type errors by providing more specific in-template type requirements to the template type checker.\nMake the input type requirements for your own directives as specific as possible by providing template-guard functions in the directive definition.\nSee \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fguide\u002Fdirectives\u002Fstructural-directives#improving-template-type-checking-for-custom-directives\">Improving template type checking for custom directives\u003C\u002Fa> in this guide.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Ch3 id=\"strict-null-checks\">\n \u003Ca href=\"#strict-null-checks\" class=\"docs-anchor\" tabindex=\"-1\" aria-label=\"Link to Strict null checks\">Strict null checks\u003C\u002Fa>\n \u003C\u002Fh3>\n \u003Cp>When you enable \u003Ccode>strictTemplates\u003C\u002Fcode> and the TypeScript flag \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode>, typecheck errors might occur for certain situations that might not easily be avoided.\nFor example:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Cul class=\"docs-list\">\n \u003Cli>\u003Cp>A nullable value that is bound to a directive from a library which did not have \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode> enabled.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>For a library compiled without \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode>, its declaration files will not indicate whether a field can be \u003Ccode>null\u003C\u002Fcode> or not.\nFor situations where the library handles \u003Ccode>null\u003C\u002Fcode> correctly, this is problematic, as the compiler will check a nullable value against the declaration files which omit the \u003Ccode>null\u003C\u002Fcode> type.\nAs such, the compiler produces a type-check error because it adheres to \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003C\u002Fli>\n\u003Cli>\u003Cp>Using the \u003Ccode>async\u003C\u002Fcode> pipe with an Observable which you know will emit synchronously.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>The \u003Ccode>async\u003C\u002Fcode> pipe currently assumes that the Observable it subscribes to can be asynchronous, which means that it's possible that there is no value available yet.\nIn that case, it still has to return something —which is \u003Ccode>null\u003C\u002Fcode>.\nIn other words, the return type of the \u003Ccode>async\u003C\u002Fcode> pipe includes \u003Ccode>null\u003C\u002Fcode>, which might result in errors in situations where the Observable is known to emit a non-nullable value synchronously.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003C\u002Fli>\n\n \u003C\u002Ful>\n \u003Cp>There are two potential workarounds to the preceding issues:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Cul class=\"docs-list\">\n \u003Cli>In the template, include the non-null assertion operator \u003Ccode>!\u003C\u002Fcode> at the end of a nullable expression, such as\u003C\u002Fli>\n\n \u003C\u002Ful>\n \u003Cdiv class=\"docs-code\">\n \n \u003Cpre class=\"shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark\" style=\"--shiki-light:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8;--shiki-light-bg:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e\" tabindex=\"0\">\u003Ccode>\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&lt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">user-detail\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0\"> [user]\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">=\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#032F62;--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF\">\"user!\"\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;&lt;\u002F\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">user-detail\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fpre>\n \u003C\u002Fdiv>\u003Cp>In this example, the compiler disregards type incompatibilities in nullability, just as in TypeScript code.\nIn the case of the \u003Ccode>async\u003C\u002Fcode> pipe, notice that the expression needs to be wrapped in parentheses, as in\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cdiv class=\"docs-code\">\n \n \u003Cpre class=\"shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark\" style=\"--shiki-light:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8;--shiki-light-bg:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e\" tabindex=\"0\">\u003Ccode>\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&lt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">user-detail\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0\"> [user]\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">=\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#032F62;--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF\">\"(user$ | async)!\"\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;&lt;\u002F\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">user-detail\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fpre>\n \u003C\u002Fdiv>\n \u003Cul class=\"docs-list\">\n \u003Cli>\u003Cp>Disable strict null checks in Angular templates completely.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>When \u003Ccode>strictTemplates\u003C\u002Fcode> is enabled, it is still possible to disable certain aspects of type checking.\nSetting the option \u003Ccode>strictNullInputTypes\u003C\u002Fcode> to \u003Ccode>false\u003C\u002Fcode> disables strict null checks within Angular templates.\nThis flag applies for all components that are part of the application.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003C\u002Fli>\n\n \u003C\u002Ful>\n \n \u003Ch3 id=\"advice-for-library-authors\">\n \u003Ca href=\"#advice-for-library-authors\" class=\"docs-anchor\" tabindex=\"-1\" aria-label=\"Link to Advice for library authors\">Advice for library authors\u003C\u002Fa>\n \u003C\u002Fh3>\n \u003Cp>As a library author, you can take several measures to provide an optimal experience for your users.\nFirst, enabling \u003Ccode>strictNullChecks\u003C\u002Fcode> and including \u003Ccode>null\u003C\u002Fcode> in an input's type, as appropriate, communicates to your consumers whether they can provide a nullable value or not.\nAdditionally, it is possible to provide type hints that are specific to the template type checker.\nSee \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fguide\u002Fdirectives\u002Fstructural-directives#improving-template-type-checking-for-custom-directives\">Improving template type checking for custom directives\u003C\u002Fa>, and \u003Ca href=\"#input-setter-coercion\">Input setter coercion\u003C\u002Fa>.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Ch2 id=\"input-setter-coercion\">\n \u003Ca href=\"#input-setter-coercion\" class=\"docs-anchor\" tabindex=\"-1\" aria-label=\"Link to Input setter coercion\">Input setter coercion\u003C\u002Fa>\n \u003C\u002Fh2>\n \u003Cp>Occasionally it is desirable for the \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002Finput\">\u003Ccode>input()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa> property of a directive or component to alter the value bound to it, typically using a \u003Ccode>transform\u003C\u002Fcode> function for the input.\nAs an example, consider this custom button component:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>Consider the following directive:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cdiv class=\"docs-code\">\n \n \u003Cpre class=\"shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark\" of the component is being passed on to the \u003Ccode>&lt;button&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode> in the template.\nAll of this works as expected, as long as a \u003Ccode>boolean\u003C\u002Fcode> value is bound to the input.\nBut, suppose a consumer uses this input in the template as an attribute:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cdiv class=\"docs-code\">\n \n \u003Cpre class=\"shiki shiki-themes github-light href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fforms\u002Fsignals\u002Fsubmit\">submit\u003C\u002Fa>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">-button\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan binding:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cdiv class=\"docs-code\">\n \n \u003Cpre class=\"shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark\" style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&lt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Ca style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\" href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fforms\u002Fsignals\u002Fsubmit\">submit\u003C\u002Fa>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">-button\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0\"> [disabled]\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">=\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#032F62;--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF\">\"''\"\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;&lt;\u002F\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Ca style=\"--shiki-light:#22863A;--shiki-dark:#85E89D\">-button\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">&gt;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fpre>\n \u003C\u002Fdiv>\u003Cp>At runtime, the input will be set to the empty string, which is not a \u003Ccode>boolean\u003C\u002Fcode> value.\nAngular component libraries that deal with this problem often \"coerce\" the value into the right type in the setter:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cdiv class=\"docs-code\">\n \n \u003Cpre class=\"shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark\" style=\"--shiki-light:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8;--shiki-light-bg:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e\" tabindex=\"0\">\u003Ccode>\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">set \u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0\">disabled\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">(value: boolean) {\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\n\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF\"> this\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">._disabled \u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583\">=\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\"> (value \u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583\">===\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#032F62;--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF\"> ''\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">) \u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583\">||\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\"> value;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\n\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">}\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fpre>\n \u003C\u002Fdiv>\u003Cp>It would be ideal to change the type of \u003Ccode>value\u003C\u002Fcode> here, from \u003Ccode>boolean\u003C\u002Fcode> to \u003Ccode>boolean|&#39;&#39;\u003C\u002Fcode>, to match the set of values which are actually accepted by the setter.\nTypeScript prior to version 4.3 requires that both the getter and setter have the same type, so if the getter should return a \u003Ccode>boolean\u003C\u002Fcode> then the setter is stuck with the narrower type.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>If the consumer has Angular's strictest type checking for templates enabled, this creates a problem: the empty string (\u003Ccode>&#39;&#39;\u003C\u002Fcode>) is not actually assignable to the \u003Ccode>disabled\u003C\u002Fcode> field, which creates a type error when the attribute form is used.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>As a workaround for this problem, Angular supports checking a wider, more permissive type for \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002FInput\">\u003Ccode>@Input()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa> than is declared for the input field itself.\nEnable this by adding a static property with the \u003Ccode>ngAcceptInputType_\u003C\u002Fcode> prefix to the component class:\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cdiv class=\"docs-code\">\n \n \u003Cpre class=\"shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark\" style=\"--shiki-light:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8;--shiki-light-bg:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e\" tabindex=\"0\">\u003Ccode>\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583\">class\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0\"> style=\"--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583\">:\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF\"> boolean\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583\"> |\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#032F62;--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF\"> ''\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">;\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\n\u003Cspan class=\"line\">\u003Cspan style=\"--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8\">}\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fspan>\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fpre>\n \u003C\u002Fdiv>\u003Cp>Since TypeScript 4.3, the setter could have been declared to accept \u003Ccode>boolean|&#39;&#39;\u003C\u002Fcode> as type, making the input setter coercion field obsolete.\nAs such, input setters coercion fields have been deprecated.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>This field does not need to have a value.\nIts existence communicates to the Angular type checker that the \u003Ccode>disabled\u003C\u002Fcode> input should be considered as accepting bindings that match the type \u003Ccode>boolean|&#39;&#39;\u003C\u002Fcode>.\nThe suffix should be the \u003Ca href=\"\u002Fapi\u002Fcore\u002FInput\">\u003Ccode>@Input\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa> \u003Cem>field\u003C\u002Fem> name.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>Care should be taken that if an \u003Ccode>ngAcceptInputType_\u003C\u002Fcode> override is present for a given input, then the setter should be able to handle any values of the overridden type.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\n \u003Ch2 id=\"disabling-type-checking-using-any\">\n \u003Ca href=\"#disabling-type-checking-using-any\" class=\"docs-anchor\" tabindex=\"-1\" aria-label=\"Link to Disabling type checking using $any()\">Disabling type checking using \u003Ccode>$any()\u003C\u002Fcode>\u003C\u002Fa>\n \u003C\u002Fh2>\n \u003Cp>Disable checking of a binding expression by surrounding the expression in a call to the \u003Ccode>$any()\u003C\u002Fcode> cast pseudo-function.\nThe compiler treats it as a cast to the \u003Ccode>any\u003C\u002Fcode> type just like in TypeScript when a \u003Ccode>&lt;any&gt;\u003C\u002Fcode> or \u003Ccode>as any\u003C\u002Fcode> cast is used.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cp>In the following example, casting \u003Ccode>person\u003C\u002Fcode> to the \u003Ccode>any\u003C\u002Fcode> type suppresses the error \u003Ccode>Property address does not exist\u003C\u002Fcode>.\u003C\u002Fp>\n\u003Cdiv class=\"docs-code\">\n \n \u003Cpre class=\"shiki
